title: LEGO Pokémon gifts-with-purchase could sell out before deadline
summary: Two LEGO Pokémon GWPs are officially due to end on 10 August, but with a similar offer already gone early, fans are being urged not to wait.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
LEGO's current run of Pokémon gifts-with-purchase (GWPs) is thinning out fast. The 40896 The X-Files: Scully's Lab GWP has officially sold out early across the UK, US and Europe, ahead of its planned end date.

Two other Pokémon-related GWPs are still up for grabs, but their official offer window is also due to close on 10 August:

- **40887 Ditto as Squirtle: Movie Night** – available worldwide (UK/US/EU) when spending £115 / $130 / €130 or more on Pokémon SMART play sets.
- **40892 Kanto Region Badge Collection** – available in the US only, with the purchase of 72153 Venusaur, Charizard and Blastoise.

LEGO GWP offers always run "while stocks last," so an official end date doesn't guarantee availability right up until then.

## Why it matters
GWPs like these are a popular way for collectors to bulk out a Pokémon or wider LEGO collection without buying an extra set outright. Given how quickly the X-Files GWP vanished, and how sought-after the Kanto badge set was on its original release, there's a real chance both remaining offers could disappear before their scheduled cut-off.

## What to watch next
If you're after either freebie, it's worth placing a qualifying order sooner rather than later. Stock levels aren't published, so once they're gone, they're gone — regardless of the official 10 August end date.

title: How big should a LEGO Lord of the Rings Helm's Deep be?
summary: With rumours swirling of a new LEGO Lord of the Rings Helm's Deep, Brick Fanatics explores what piece count would do the iconic castle justice.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
Brick Fanatics has taken a look at how large a potential new LEGO The Lord of the Rings Helm's Deep set could be, following **rumours** that LEGO may expand the theme with three new sets, including a Helm's Deep castle, possibly arriving in 2027 or 2028.

The only minifigure-scale Helm's Deep so far is the 2012 combo of 9474 The Battle of Helm's Deep and 9471 Uruk-Hai Army, totalling around 1,625 pieces — modest by today's standards. For comparison, recent flagship LEGO Lord of the Rings sets like 10316 Rivendell (around 6,000 pieces), 10333 Barad-dûr and 11377 Minas Tirith have set a much bigger benchmark.

The article points to fan-made concepts, including one from Playwell Bricks envisioning a Rivendell-scale Helm's Deep with a detailed interior and full-length wall, as an example of what an official set at that size could look like.

**Note: any new Helm's Deep set, its size, and its release window are unconfirmed rumours at this stage.**

## Why it matters
Helm's Deep is one of the most iconic locations in Middle-earth, and fans have long wanted a set that matches the scale and detail of recent Lord of the Rings flagships. If the rumours prove true, this could be a major addition for castle builders, display collectors and Lord of the Rings fans alike.

## What to watch next
Keep an eye out for any official LEGO Lord of the Rings announcements confirming a Helm's Deep set, along with details on piece count, scale and release date.

bodyMarkdown:

Jackson makes a brief cameo in the films as Albert Dreary, a rain-soaked, carrot-munching local seen in the Prancing Pony introduction sequence that every LEGO Lord of the Rings Prancing Pony-themed build has referenced. A fan-made LEGO Ideas project by ErockBrick has already shown how an Albert Dreary minifigure could fit into a Prancing Pony set, demonstrating it's a realistic and fitting inclusion if the set goes ahead.

It's worth stressing that the Prancing Pony set itself is currently just a **rumour** and hasn't been confirmed by LEGO.

## Why it matters
For Lord of the Rings fans and minifigure collectors, any hint of a Prancing Pony set is exciting, not just for the build itself but for the possibility of a rare and highly desirable minifigure making a comeback. Given how much the original Peter Jackson minifigure sold for, a new version could become one of the most sought-after inclusions in the LEGO Lord of the Rings range.

title: Fan builds tiny LEGO castle using rare Modulex bricks
summary: Builder Isaiah Kepner has created a microscale castle small enough to fit on a footprint under 4x4 studs, using LEGO's rarely-seen Modulex bricks rather than standard System pieces.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
According to The Brothers Brick, fan builder Isaiah Kepner has put together an incredibly small custom castle for the Summer Joust building event. Rather than using standard LEGO System bricks, the model is built with Modulex bricks - a smaller-scale brick range LEGO produced back in the 1960s, originally intended for architectural modelling rather than play.

The finished castle sits on a footprint reported to be a little smaller than 4x4 studs in regular System brick terms, making it genuinely tiny. The scale becomes clearer when you spot familiar reference points scattered around the landscape, such as tiles, small "antler" pieces, or even a minifigure-scale head, all of which help highlight just how small the fortress actually is next to normal parts.

Many official LEGO fan contests only allow parts made by the LEGO company itself, and Modulex technically counts, even though it's a far less common and lesser-known product line compared to standard bricks.

## Why it matters
This is a fun example of how creative fans can push scale and part choice to create something genuinely eye-catching, and it's a good reminder that LEGO's brick history goes beyond the System bricks most collectors know. For anyone into microscale builds or brick history, Modulex is a niche but interesting corner of the hobby worth knowing about.

## What to watch next
It's worth keeping an eye out for more Modulex-based creations, as builders continue to explore unusual or vintage parts for microscale and novelty builds.

The claims suggest a **Hello Kitty display model** is in the works for 2027 or 2028, echoing earlier rumours from this summer about a Sanrio-themed LEGO set. Finally, it's claimed a single **Street Fighter set** could arrive in the same 2027-2028 window, timed loosely alongside the fighting game's upcoming live-action film.

None of this has been confirmed by the LEGO Group, and as with all rumours, it should be treated with caution until an official announcement appears.

## Why it matters
If even one of these turns out to be true, it would mark a first for LEGO in terms of licensing: the brand has yet to touch fighting games despite decades of successful video game tie-ins. For UK collectors, a Knight Rider Icons set would appeal to fans of classic TV and car builds, while Hello Kitty and Street Fighter would open up entirely new pop-culture and gaming audiences to the brick hobby.

## What to watch next

title: Fan builder shares how he created a huge Wild West LEGO diorama

bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
The Brothers Brick has published a guest feature from builder Evan Crouch, known online as evanceltlego, detailing how he created a large Wild West-themed LEGO railroad diorama for the Rocky Mountain Train Show in Colorado.

According to the piece, Crouch wanted a mostly tiled layout with only a few studs visible, and aimed to capture the banded rock layers seen in nearby Utah's mountain buttes. He settled on a big 7x5 baseplate layout (35 baseplates in total, working out to 224 x 160 studs) sized to fit R72 train track, designed so local LUG members could each add their own sections to build a huge collaborative display.

He planned the project using Google Sheets to map out the layout and Studio software to test colour combinations, eventually settling on a western-inspired palette including tan, warm tan, dark tan, medium nougat, dark red, dark orange, bright light yellow, bright light orange, sand blue and reddish brown. Crouch created a 'strata map' to keep the layered rock colours consistent across different builders' sections, favouring cheaper, easier-to-source colours for the bulk of the terrain.

Sourcing the huge number of curved slopes and tiles needed took several months, using BrickLink and LEGO's online Pick A Brick service, including hunting down newer elements like warm tan pieces and printed tan tiles from recent sets.

## Why it matters
This is a great example of how much planning goes into a large-scale collaborative LEGO display, from colour theory and part-sourcing to coordinating with other builders.
